notes.meaning: John sees a mighty angel come down from heaven wrapped in a cloud, crowned with a rainbow, and shining like the sun with feet of fire. The cloud points to God's holy majesty and coming judgment, while the rainbow recalls His promise of mercy. Even when fierce troubles shake the earth, God reminds His people that He remains in faithful control.

differ.view: The angel is most likely the Lord Jesus Christ himself, veiling a glory too great for human eyes.
Early Methodist teaching holds he is a created angel. He swears by God rather than by himself, and this kind of glory is not too much for a creature.
He is a created angel, perhaps Michael, since Christ does not come down to earth until chapter 19.

notes.meaning: The angel holds a small, open scroll and places one foot on the ocean and the other on dry ground. Standing over both sea and land shows that God has rightful authority over the whole created world. The open scroll reveals that God is about to make His secret plans clear to His people.

The angel calls out with a mighty shout that sounds like the roar of a lion. When he cries out, seven thunders answer with distinct voices. In Scripture, thunder often pictures the voice of the Lord speaking with awe and authority.

differ.view: Some older Protestant teachers read this chapter as a picture of the Reformation. In that reading, the seven thunders are the Pope's condemnations sent out from Rome, the city of seven hills.

notes.meaning: John gets ready to write down what the seven thunders said, but a voice from heaven orders him to keep it secret. God reveals much about the future, yet He chooses to leave some things hidden in His own wisdom. Believers can trust that God knows what is best to reveal and what is best to keep quiet.

differ.view: Some who read Revelation as mostly future events say the setting suggests the thunders are about the coming bowl judgments of chapter 16, while still warning against guessing.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some modern scholars suggest this command explains why the author chose to leave out an existing set of seven thunder prophecies known in his day.

notes.meaning: The glorious angel standing over the sea and the land raises his right hand toward heaven. In Bible times, lifting a hand was the standard way to swear a solemn oath before God. This action shows that what the angel is about to announce is completely certain.

The angel swears by the eternal God, who created the heavens, the earth, the sea, and everything in them. He declares that there will be no more delay in finishing God's work. The same almighty power that made the world will bring history to its appointed close.

When the seventh angel is ready to blow his trumpet, God's mystery will be finished. A mystery in the Bible means a truth once hidden that God has now made known to people. This fulfilling of His plan matches everything God promised long ago through His servants the prophets.

The heavenly voice speaks to John a second time and tells him to go to the angel. John must step forward and take the open scroll directly from the angel's hand. God invites His servants to take an active part in receiving and sharing His word.

John asks for the scroll, and the angel tells him to take it and eat it. Eating the scroll is a picture of taking God's truth deep into the heart and thinking about it carefully. The angel warns him that while the message will taste as sweet as honey, it will turn his stomach bitter.

John takes the scroll and eats it, finding that it tastes sweet in his mouth but makes his stomach bitter. God's message brings sweet joy because it promises the final victory of His kingdom. At the same time, it brings bitter sorrow because it speaks of painful judgments and suffering for the world.

The angel tells John that he must prophesy again to many peoples, nations, languages, and rulers. To prophesy means to proclaim God's truth and reveal what He will do. God's message is not just for one group of believers, but speaks to the whole world.
